Dear Statnet List,

Please pass around; the dates seem a little odd, but we have to get 
official permission from NIH to roll over funds, which are granted on a 
yearly basis.

Best
Simon

***

UNIVERSITY OF CAMBRIDGE

DEPARTMENT OF VETERINARY MEDICINE

Research Associate in Network Epidemiology and Respondent Driven Sampling

Stipend ?27,183.00 to ?35,469.00

Limit of Tenure: 30 April 2010 with reappointment on a yearly basis to 
30 April 2012.

Respondent-driven sampling (http://www.respondentdrivensampling.org), 
RDS. is a sampling method that is being increasingly used to sample 
?hidden? populations such as injection drug users, the homeless, 
commercial sex workers, and men who have sex with men. RDS involves 
individuals recruiting peers from their social network, and consequently 
provides rich information on social networks, as well as providing means 
of obtaining (in principle) unbiased estimates of quantities such the 
prevalence of infectious diseases.

This project, in collaboration with Douglas Heckathorn at Cornell, the 
original developer of RDS, involves the development of statistical, 
computational, and mathematical models of social networks and respondent 
driven sampling. These models will be applied to several datasets 
collected by our collaborators from different hidden populations worldwide.

You should have a PhD in one of the following fields: statistics, 
computational biology, sociology, mathematics, or epidemiology. You 
should have a keen interest in social/sexual/drug-using networks. You 
should also have excellent quantitative skills, be proficient in 
computer programming (R, C/C++, Python), or show evidence that such 
skills can be acquired quickly.

For informal enquiries contact Dr. Simon Frost by email: sdf22@cam.ac.uk

Further particulars are available at: http://www.vet.cam.ac.uk/news/

Applicants should supply the following:

Letter of application stating areas of interest
Curriculum Vitae, with the names and contact details of three referees
A completed application form PD18, (parts one and three only) available 
from the Melissa Large on 01223 337055 or from:
http://www.admin.cam.ac.uk/offices/hr/forms/pd18

Applications should be sent to Melissa Large, Department of Veterinary 
Medicine, Madingley Road, Cambridge CB3 0ES to arrive no later than 1st 
March 2010. Applications can be made via email to recruit@vet.cam.ac.uk 
with the above documents as word attachments. Interviews will be held in 
19th March 2010.

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simulate and estimate ERGM with missing edges?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Simulate and estimate ERGM with missing edges?
messages.body_plain:
Hi--

Is there any reason why I shouldn't be able to simulate ERGM(THETA0), sample a subgraph of the network, and the estimate the ERGM(THETA0) with 'NA's where the edges are missing (a la Handcock and Giles)?

I am trying to simulate and estimate any undirected network more exotic than "edges," perhaps "edges + triangles + kstars(3)" or other statistics that don't suffer from high collinearity (Snijders finds edges, triangles, and kstars to be highly collinear).

I really just want to simulate and estimate any ERGM(THETA0) model to see if I can get the parameters back and what their finite sample distribution looks like. I have taken a look at mcmc.diagnostics(), but even when it says that things have converged, I still have issues. I have also tried a variety of values of THETA0, to attempt to produce only slight deviations from the "edges" model. However, I consistently end up with degenerate matrices and ERGM crashes.

Any advice on how to get things to estimate properly? Do I need really, really large burn-ins and MCMCsamplesizes with large sampling intervals? Or can those exacerbate my estimation problems? Do I need large networks to ensure that I have enough edges, or would smaller networks work better for this simulation exercise?

Thanks!

--Randall

messages.subject: [statnet_help] Simulate and estimate ERGM with missing edges?
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] Simulate and estimate ERGM with missing edges?
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Randall.  Have you verified that you are getting the correct mean 
stats (i.e., that your simulated mean statistics match the observed 
statistics) for your model _without_ adding the missing data?  If your 
model is borderline-degenerate (as most regular models based on 
triangles/k-stars are), then this could be the root of your problem. 
Alternately, the algorithm may not have converged closely enough for 
your needs.  MCMC diagnostics are helpful here, but are not a substitute 
for making sure that you have convergence in mean value space; if not, 
you may need to increase the number of iterations of the fitting 
procedure.  (Remember that the likelihood surface is being approximated 
via a finite-sample Monte Carlo procedure, and even a "clean" sample 
will leave some approximation error, especially if the starting value 
was far from the true MLE.)

Some current work by Arthur Asuncion appears to suggest that greatly 
increasing the number of fitting iterations (the ergm maxit argument) 
can result in improved performance, even if the quality and size of each 
MCMC sample is reduced.  This is still an area of active research, but 
my informal experimentation with this type of approach has been pretty 
consistent with his initial findings.  If you want to experiment with 
this approach, try greatly reducing the burn-in, thinning, and sample 
size parameters, and increase maxit correspondingly (e.g., on the order 
of 100-500).  Purely anecdotally, my experience was that this worked 
surprisingly well at getting close to the MLE, but that getting 
high-precision convergence required boosting the MCMC sample quality 
back up.  (There are good reasons to expect this kind of behavior, as 
Arthur has pointed out.)  Also, bear in mind that for goodness-of-fit 
assessment, you really need a high-quality sample.

To sum up:

1. If your model doesn't work in the complete data case, it is unlikely 
to work otherwise.  So check that first, if you haven't already.

2. If your MCMC samples are good, then the problem may be that you need 
more "outer" iterations of the fitting procedure to get convergence to 
the true MLE.  If the mean stats from a high quality MCMC sample at the 
estimated MLE don't closely match your observed stats, the model has not 
converged.

3. On the other end of things, it is possible to get MCMC samples that 
appear to have converged based on casual inspection, but have that are 
still far from equilibrium.  (Note that I am speaking of the Markov 
chain per se, not the entire MLE estimation process.)  Increasing 
burn/thin/sample size parameters can help with this, as might switching 
to another MCMC proposal distribution.  See also any good applied MCMC 
text (e.g., Gilks et al.) for advice on convergence assessment/improvement.


Oh, one other thing: given a draw, g, from an ERG(theta) distribution, 
there is no guarantee that MLE(g) exists.  (Indeed, for graphs of finite 
order, there will usually be a positive probability that the MLE will 
not exist.)  That's because there is a positive probability of drawing 
some g that is on the edge of the convex hull of possible values for the 
sufficient statistics (as opposed to being in the relative interior), 
and the MLE in this case will diverge for some or all of the model 
parameters.  For some models, this contingency is remote: the 
probability of drawing a "defective" g is so tiny that you'll never run 
into one.  (E.g., a pure edges model with parameter 0 on a graph of 
order >>10.)  For models with "extreme" choices of theta, for which the 
underlying statistics interact in funny ways, or for very small graphs, 
this can happen much more often.  If you are finding that your 
simulate/refit process usually works, but occasionally produces models 
with divergent MLEs, this could be the culprit.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

fact, my attributes are of two categories A and B. So the 2-mode
matrix is of the form Ox(A,B), i.e., to any object o in O it may

assistance.

Best,

--Moses

messages.subject: [statnet_help] A question about running ergm on 2-mode networks
messages.subject_clean: [statnet_help] A question about running ergm on 2-mode networks
messages.body_plain:
Moses,

If I understand correctly, you want to create a social network of objects, where the relationship defining a link is their shared value of an attribute in A.  You then want to create a second social network of objects, where the relationship defining a link is their shared value of an attribute in B.  Then, you want to see if one the two networks is a significant predictor of link formation in the other.

To create a network, where the relationship is based on their shared attribute, take the vector of length O consisting of attributes A (we'll call this X).  Take the dot product of X.Xtranspose.  This will create a social network of size O by O, where there is a link if two nodes share the same attribute in A.  Repeat the same process for O and B.

To see if one network is significant in the ergm model for another, use edgecov().  

Depending on the nature of the attribute, it may be more interesting to see how different they are.  For example if your O by A vector was {2,5,9}, you could take differences to get the network {0,-3,-7}{3,0,-4}{7,4,0} or something.

If you want to see how similar two objects are across multiple attributes, then Ox(A,B)*(A,B)xO will give you an OxO where the link weight is the shared number of attributes.  This is what I typically do for homophily.

Best of luck.

Ian

messages.body_plain:
Hi,

in case someone starts writing a read.dl or write.dl function: It may be 
worthwhile writing a read.ucinet or write.ucinet function instead which 
reads the native (binary) file format of Ucinet (the .##h. and ##d 
files). Here are some details about the file format:

The ##d file:
- the 'data' file which contains all the cell entries of the adjacency 
matrix. They are not separated by any character. Each cell entry is 
encoded as a 32 bit float number according to the IEEE-754 standard and 
with little endian encoding. For example, a weight in the adjacency 
matrix of '3' is saved as the hex value '00 00 80 3F'.

The ##h file:
- the header file which contains the row and column labels
- starts with the hex value '05'
- then '44 41 54 45 3A' (which means 'DATE:' in ASCII)
- then some code I haven't been able to figure out yet (probably a 
date..., perhaps the authors of Ucinet are able to help here)
- then the row labels as ASCII code (separated by '00 00' in hex code)
- and finally the network label in ASCII.
- of course, the structure may be different if we are talking about 
two-mode networks etc.

If anyone in the statnet team or elsewhere is interested in writing a 
read.ucinet function (which is probably something many people would be 
interested in), it might be a good idea to start out with a hex editor 
and reproduce the above steps.

Take care

Philip

On Wed, Feb 10, 2010 at 10:39 AM, Philip Leifeld <Leifeld@coll.mpg.de>wrote:

> Hi,
>
> in case someone starts writing a read.dl or write.dl function: It may be
> worthwhile writing a read.ucinet or write.ucinet function instead which
> reads the native (binary) file format of Ucinet (the .##h. and ##d files).
> Here are some details about the file format:
>
> The ##d file:
> - the 'data' file which contains all the cell entries of the adjacency
> matrix. They are not separated by any character. Each cell entry is encoded
> as a 32 bit float number according to the IEEE-754 standard and with little
> endian encoding. For example, a weight in the adjacency matrix of '3' is
> saved as the hex value '00 00 80 3F'.
>
> The ##h file:
> - the header file which contains the row and column labels
> - starts with the hex value '05'
> - then '44 41 54 45 3A' (which means 'DATE:' in ASCII)
> - then some code I haven't been able to figure out yet (probably a date...,
> perhaps the authors of Ucinet are able to help here)
> - then the row labels as ASCII code (separated by '00 00' in hex code)
> - and finally the network label in ASCII.
> - of course, the structure may be different if we are talking about
> two-mode networks etc.
>
> If anyone in the statnet team or elsewhere is interested in writing a
> read.ucinet function (which is probably something many people would be
> interested in), it might be a good idea to start out with a hex editor and
> reproduce the above steps.
>
> Take care
>
> Philip

messages.subject: [statnet_help] GWESP - parameter setting
messages.body_plain:
> However, I do not fully understand what is captured by the scaling parameter 
> alpha (or lambda?). If I do not fix this parameter (i.e. the default 
> setting), the model fit as indicated by AIC and BIC is quite good, but the 
> graphical goodness of fit assessment does *not* look very nice. If I fix the 
> parameter at 0 or 0.1, the gof is really good, but AIC and BIC are much

Hello Philip,

This is a good (and common question) - thanks for asking it, and sorry for the delay in response.

This parameter and its interpretation is discussed in a few of our group's papers, but generally only very briefly.  Moreover, its parameterization has varied from paper to paper so it can be particularly confusing.  One way I like to think of it is as follows - we believe there is a tendency for triangles to close (assuming we're testing for a positive coefficient here, as we usually are).  Or, equivalently, we believe there is a tendency for those with shared partners to become tied.  We might imagine that this effect is stronger the greater the number of shared partners two people have.  That effect could be linear in the number of shared partners, or it could take some other parametric or non-parametric form.  GWESP assumes a parametric form in which there are declining marginal returns to tie probability across different numbers of shared partners.  The scaling parameter that you asked 
about controls that rate of declining marginal returns; the GWESP coefficient controls the overall strength of triad close given that rate.

It helps to think of the extremes. When the scaling parameter equals 0, nothing beyond the first shared partner matters; thus, the statistic becomes equivalent to the number of edges that are in at least one triangle. When it approaches in finity, there is no decline; all triangles matter equally no matter how many other triangles two of their actors are in, and the statistic approaches three times the number of triangles. In general, the lower the value of the scaling parameter, the less likely the model is to be degenerate.

One can allow ergm to estimate the parameter from the data (using fixed=FALSE), although this generally greatly increases the estimation time one needs in order to ensure convergence.  Or, one can can use fixed=TRUE and simply estimate the coefficient for a single scaling parameter, if one either has a priori information about what the scaling parameter should be, or is willing to make an assumption.  In practice I have found that it seems to matter relatively little what specific value I use in the range of 0-1.5 or so on a variety of networks.

As for your observation that the AIC and BIC get better when the GOF plots get worse. I don't have much specific insight on that, other than to say that they are measuring different features of model fit (the GOF plots are generally focusing on more global features depending on which you are using) and we still have a long way to go to understand all of the ways that global structure emerges from local network process. If you have more information to help us understand your specific case, I'd love to hear it.

Cheers,
Steve

messages.subject: [statnet_help] GWESP - parameter setting
messages.body_plain:
Hi, Steve.  Just to chime in on this -

Steven Goodreau wrote:
> As for your observation that the AIC and BIC get better when the GOF 
> plots get worse. I don't have much specific insight on that, other than 
> to say that they are measuring different features of model fit (the GOF 
> plots are generally focusing on more global features depending on which 
> you are using) and we still have a long way to go to understand all of 
> the ways that global structure emerges from local network process. If 
> you have more information to help us understand your specific case, I'd 
> love to hear it.

In my experience, that's usually a sign of poor mixing.  The AIC/BIC are 
based on the estimated likelihood, which is fairly sensitive to the size 
and quality of the MCMC sample.  A poorly mixed sample can lead to an 
erroneously high likelihood, but tends to show itself in the diagnostics 
(both ours and the MCMC diagnostics one gets from e.g., coda).  Adding a 
high-dependence statistic can thus lead to an apparent improvement in 
fit, due not to an actual impact on model performance, but to the fact 
that it cripples the underling Markov chain.  Careful attention to the 
diagnostics is, as always, the best defense.

Hope that helps,

-Carter

PS. Of course, the GOF plots are also sample-dependent, so it is 
important to inspect those MCMC diagnostics as well.  One would hate to 
propose a good model, only to accidentally reject it due to skimping on 
the validation sample!
